newsitem.title: UK: Belize PM sees extreme harm if banana exports hurt.
newsitem.headline: Belize PM sees extreme harm if banana exports hurt.

text.p: Belize Prime Minister Manuel Esquivel warned on Wednesday in London of extreme damage to Caribbean countries if preferential treatment of banana exports to the European Union was scrapped.

"Bananas play a vital role in the economies of Belize...The action initiated by the U.S. at the WTO (World Trade Organisation) would, if successful, prove extremely damaging to all Caribbean producing countries," Esquivel said.

Esquivel, on a visit in London to meet British Foreign Secretary Malcom Rifkind and Agricultural Minister Douglas Hogg, has been fighting U.S.-backed Latin American proposal to the WTO to end the Caribbean's preferential access to the EU market.
Marijuana, Esquivel said, could be an alternative for the weaker of the producing countries if banana export was hit.
"For the Windward Islands, I doubt even given time they would be able to identify alternatives, at least not legal ones. There's always the possibility of marijuana," he told reporters.
"They don't have to fight tariff barriers, they don't have to worry about finding markets, it's all set up, it wil be very lucrative," Esquivel said.
He attacked multinational trading companies for trying to push the Caribbean countries, which produce bananas at greater costs, off the playing field.
"It is only the United States multi-national, Chiquita, all of whose plantations are outside the United States, that is complaining," he said.
"They obviously have tremendous influence in the United States government," he said.
Banana export represented six percent of the gross domestic product of Belize, but only two percent of EU consumption, he said.
Four Latin American countries -- Ecuador, Honduras, Guatemala and Mexico -- and the United States, a non-exporting country, complained in May that EU banana rules were discriminatory.
The EU rules, came into force in 1993 under the Lome Convention, were aimed at benefitting ACP countries.
Esquivel said the group of small Caribbean countries were no match for the producers in Latin American countries.
"Level playing field is not the guarantee of fairness."
